# Orchestrate Verification

Coordinate agents to make measurable progress on verification and
synchronization objectives. Run a long-lived campaign as a sequence of bounded
objectives, checkpointing after each objective so execution may stop safely at
any time. Expect that you will run for several hours before a human kills your
process or asks you to stop. To continue later where you left off, continually
record your progress using branches, PRs, issues, and discussions on this twin
repository.

In this skill:

- **Twin repository** means `https://github.com/jaylorch/nvx-verified-twin`.
- **Upstream repository** means `https://github.com/microsoft/nvx`.
- **Verus repository** means `https://github.com/verus-lang/verus`.

The long-term goals are:

1. Prove important high-level properties of the code under `openvmm/`.
2. Work toward a state where twin `openvmm/` matches upstream NVX, except for
   verification annotations and the smallest necessary proof-only support.
3. Work toward a state where twin `verus/` matches the Verus repository.

Temporary divergence is allowed when it enables active verification work, carries a
needed fix while its upstream or Verus pull request is pending, or is otherwise
necessary to make progress. Treat such divergence as tracked integration debt, not a
permanent fork: document its reason and corresponding revision or pull request,
minimize its scope, periodically reassess whether it is still needed, and converge
back to the corresponding repository when the pull request is resolved or the need
disappears. A pending pull request may justify the twin carrying its proposed fix
before the corresponding repository does; a merged or rejected pull request may not
remain indefinitely as the justification for that difference.

When posting to an issue using a human's credentials, clearly note at the
beginning of the post that it was generated by an AI agent. When submitting a
PR using a human's credentials, clearly note at the beginning of the PR body
that the PR was generated by an AI agent.

When you need help from a human, create an issue in the twin repository with
the label "human needed". For instance, you will need help from a human to
open a PR on a different repository such as the upstream repository or the
Verus repository.

Do not ask for human help before making changes to the twin repository; just
change the twin repository however you feel appropriate. More generally, do
not ask for permission to make reversible decisions that only affect the twin
repository; just make those decisions yourself. Eventually, if you discover
unwise decisions, just undo them.

Before mutating GitHub, confirm the exact target repository and search for an
existing issue or PR to avoid duplicates. Link mutations to the campaign issue
and use the repository's established promotion or synchronization workflow.

## 1. Establish A Bounded Objective

Inspect open verification issues and current repository divergence to choose
what your multiple sub-agents should work on. Run those multiple sub-agents in
parallel with each other, making sure they're working on non-conflicting
goals. Do not pause to ask which issues or objectives to work on; that's your
choice.

Anchor every campaign in a GitHub issue in the twin repository. For instance,
if you decide to work on some divergence of the current repository, create an
issue for it first. And, if handling an open verification issue requires
multiple steps, work on those steps one at a time, recording progress in the
issue comments. Discuss clarifications, scope choices, and other questions in
that issue rather than in ephemeral agent chat.

Proceed autonomously on reversible technical decisions and twin-local work.
Sub-agents may investigate uncertain technical questions and recommend an
answer, but their guesses do not grant authorization. Do not guess when a
decision would materially expand scope, perform a destructive operation,
change product behavior without supporting evidence, or publish to a
repository not explicitly named by this skill or the objective. When necessary
authority is absent, record the blocker and continue with independent work.
Expect that humans will periodically review your code and, if they disagree
with your choices, post issues asking for corrections.

## 2. Periodically Reconcile Upstream

One of your jobs is to check for updates to the upstream repository to see
what divergence with the twin repository this caused and fix such divergence.

Keep each synchronization bounded and safe. If unrelated upstream changes make a
complete update too broad for the current campaign, record the exact drift and create
or update a focused issue to track the next synchronization.

## 3. Build A Dependency-Aware Work Plan

Decompose the objective only where work is genuinely independent. Useful roles
include:

- **Property analysis:** formalize the intended invariant and identify trusted
  assumptions.
- **Proof implementation:** add specifications, proof annotations, and lemmas.
- **Verification review:** challenge proof completeness, vacuity, and assumption
  strength.
- **Upstream comparison:** classify behavioral changes separately from proof-only
  changes.
- **Verus analysis:** minimize and isolate any verifier limitation or missing
  library specification.

Assign each task a bounded scope, expected output, and stop condition. Record
actual dependencies, start only ready work, and run independent,
non-conflicting tasks in parallel. Avoid assigning multiple agents to edit the
same files or solve the same question.

When delegating, choose models by task:

- Use **Astra** (`gpt-6-astra`) for high-level property formalization, trusted-boundary
  analysis, and overall proof strategy.
- Use **Sol** (`gpt-6-sol`) to implement or debug Verus specifications and proofs.
- Use **Luna** (`gpt-6-luna`) for bounded mechanical work such as scripts, tests, and
  comparing repository revisions or files.

If a model is unavailable or unsuitable for a task, use the available model
best suited to that task.

If the orchestrator adds new skill files to enable verification agents, place them
under `.github/skills/verification/`. Give each skill its own appropriately named
subdirectory and `SKILL.md`; do not place verification-specific skills elsewhere in
`.github/skills/`.

The orchestrator owns integration and all shared state. Agents report results directly
to the orchestrator. Do not use GitHub issues or pull requests as ephemeral
agent-to-agent messaging, and do not allow concurrent agents to mutate the same
branch, issue, or pull request.

## 4. Triage Verification Work

For proof requests:

1. State the high-level property in plain language and identify the observable
   behavior it constrains.
2. Locate the narrowest trusted boundary and existing specifications or assumptions.
3. Put reusable formalizations in `openvmm/verification/specs/`. For example, define
   a `spec fn f_postcondition(...)` there and attach
   `ensures f_postcondition(...)` to `f` at its implementation site.
4. Use the `verus!` macro around verified code. Do not use Verus attribute syntax
   such as `#[verus_verify]` or `#[verus_spec(...)]`.
5. Your goal is to *eventually* prove correct the actual production
   implementation. But often, to make progress, it's expedient to replace a
   small part of the code with a modified version, or to mark a piece of code
   with an annotation like `#[verifier::external_body]`. Later iterations of
   your workflow should periodically detect this divergence and work to fix
   it.
6. For every proof result, record the exact source revision, modified code,
   `external_body` uses, trusted assumptions, and remaining divergence. State
   explicitly whether the property applies to the current upstream
   implementation or only to a proposed or modified implementation. Never
   present verification of a substitute implementation as verification of
   current upstream production code.

Treat expert review comments as hypotheses to validate, not instructions to apply
blindly. Reproduce the concern, make the smallest coherent correction, and preserve
the intended property.

## 5. Control Assumptions And Product Bugs

Every new assumption must be:

- Necessary for the current proof and narrower than the property being proved.
- Documented with its trusted source and the reason it cannot yet be proved.
- Added to the appropriate Rust file under
  `openvmm/verification/assumptions/`.

If work reveals a likely product bug, devise a fix to it. Then, create an
issue labeled "human needed" in which you give instructions to the human about
how to open a PR on the upstream repository to apply the fix. Include a
minimal reproducer and evidence that distinguishes the bug from a
specification or verifier error. Also, apply that fix to the twin repository,
accompanied by a comment linking to the "human needed" issue just created.
Applying that fix to the twin repository will create a temporary divergence
that should eventually get fixed, after the human creates the PR and
disposition of that PR is resolved.

Sometimes you may discover a code hygiene issue that isn't a bug but
complicates verification, such as a function being several pages long. If the
code-hygiene fix seems helpful enough that the developer will likely
appreciate it happening in the main repository, treat it like a bug. That is,
devise a fix, post a "human needed" issue, and apply it to the twin repository
while you wait for the human-led PR process.

If a Verus limitation blocks an important goal, first minimize it and rule out
a sound local proof or library specification. When a Verus change is
necessary, prepare the smallest general fix and do two things with it. First,
create an issue labeled "human needed". In that issue, give instructions to
the human about how to open a PR in the Verus repository to apply the fix.
Second, apply that fix in the twin repository under `verus/`, along with a
source code comment linking to the "human needed" issue just created.
Performing the local change will create a temporary divergence that should
eventually get fixed, after the human creates the PR and its disposition is
resolved.

## 6. Reconcile Repository Divergence

Compare explicit revisions rather than mutable branch names alone. Classify each
difference as:

- Proof annotation or proof-only support.
- Necessary temporary divergence with a documented reason and convergence path.
- Pending upstream or Verus change with a linked pull request.
- Unintentional behavioral divergence.

Do not compare only file names or diff size. Never discard verification work
to make a textual diff smaller.

For every temporary divergence, record what must happen before it can be
removed. Remove obsolete divergence promptly.

For an outstanding pull request, check its exact head revision, review and CI state,
mergeability, and whether the local change is source-equivalent. Reconcile every
terminal outcome:

- **Merged:** update from the corresponding repository through the established
  promotion workflow, confirm the accepted fix is present, and remove any redundant
  twin-only copy or workaround.
- **Rejected or closed without merge:** review the disposition and resolve the local
  discrepancy. Remove or revise the twin-only change when the proposed fix is no
  longer appropriate. If the underlying bug still requires a fix, address the review
  feedback and establish a new explicit convergence path, such as a replacement
  pull request; do not keep citing the closed pull request as sufficient
  justification.
- **Superseded:** link the replacement pull request, confirm which revision the twin
  carries, and retire the obsolete tracking record.

## 7. Integrate And Validate

Discover authoritative setup and validation commands from current repository
instructions, CI, and build configuration. At minimum:

1. Run the narrowest applicable Verus check after each proof change.
2. Run the package-level verification command for the affected OpenVMM code.
3. For production-code changes, run the applicable formatter, build or check,
   and tests in addition to Verus verification.
4. Re-run divergence checks against the recorded revisions after synchronization
   changes.
5. Have an independent verification review challenge the final proof when the result
   establishes a new high-level property or expands the trusted boundary.

Report unavailable tools, platforms, credentials, or host capabilities as
blocked. Never report an unrun gate as passed.

## 8. Publish Durable Checkpoints

After each bounded objective, update the campaign issue with:

- Exact revisions and working branch.
- Work completed and its evidence.
- Proof scope, trusted assumptions, and any `external_body` uses.
- Divergence introduced, retained, or removed, with its convergence path.
- Validation commands and outcomes, including unavailable gates.
- Related issues and draft PRs.
- Blockers and the next smallest actionable step.

Keep checkpoints concise but sufficient for a later agent to resume without
reconstructing state from ephemeral chat.
